Join now Activity 1K followers Posts Comments Reactions No more previous content Michael Lock Michael Lock 4mo Report this post Michael Lock posted this I spent time at a client offsite yesterday digging into the challenges and opportunities with ESG comms and more broadly, how brands talk about sustainability and social impact. Today I see a lot of brands stuck in two extremes: 1. Dense report-speak that only investors, auditors or bots will ever need to read. 2. Feel-good campaigns that gloss over the hard tradeoffs and real impact. The reality for most companies sits in the messy middle: real progress in some areas, gaps and tension in others, and stakeholders who are far more informed than they were five years ago. Against that backdrop, I see three shifts redefining the role of corporate brands in culture at a time when stakeholders are impatient for change and skeptical of purpose claims: • Brand Value → Emotional Value: People care more about how companies and brands reflect their identity and create psychological safety than about abstract “brand equity.” • Collective Action → Authentic Action: People look for a clear connection between the business and a purpose platform focused on specific issues where it brings real credibility and expertise. • Big Long-term Goals → Real Impact Now: People expect incremental progress and tangible results. They’re quick to call out “purpose washing” or “greenwashing” if claims aren’t backed by visible action. When ESG communication is treated as reputation polish, your stakeholders can smell it. When it’s treated as part of how the company is accountable to the world around it, the conversation changes....more 41 4 Comments Copy LinkedIn Facebook X Michael Lock Michael Lock 11mo Report this post Michael Lock shared this 92% of consumers say it's important for brands to communicate their sustainability efforts. Let that sink in. Nearly everyone wants to hear what your brand is doing to protect the planet—yet too often, those stories are missing, muddled, or muted. A new study from MAGNA Global and Sharethrough makes it clear: sustainability comms aren't optional—they're expected. And for communicators, this is a moment to lead with intention. Here are 3 things to keep in mind as you shape your sustainability storytelling: 1. Sustainability isn't assumed—it must be articulated. Even if your brand is doing the work, it only matters if your audience knows it. Clear, consistent messaging around sustainability efforts builds trust and sets you apart. 2. Focus on proof, not platitudes. Today's consumers are increasingly savvy and attuned to greenwashing. Back up claims with data, third-party validation, and specifics. Transparency beats perfection. 3. Tailor the message, not the mission. Sustainability means different things to different audiences. Meet people where they are, but don’t dilute the integrity of your brand’s commitment. Over the course of my career, I've had the privilege of working across some of the most diverse industries imaginable — defense, entertainment, social impact, hospitality, and everything in between. Every industry taught me something different about how people communicate, what audiences actually respond to, and how to build strategies that perform. While I always dreamed of owning my own business one day, I'll admit it came sooner than I anticipated. But when the opportunity arose, I had a choice: let the moment pass, or bet on myself. I went all in — and I didn't do it alone. There are so many people who made this possible. My mentors and clients who believed in me, gave me room to grow, make mistakes, try new things, and trusted me with their most important work. My parents, Rhod Shaw and Emily Young Shaw, who taught me that being a hard worker and a good person are never mutually exclusive, and to always pour your heart into everything you do. My brother and entrepreneurial inspiration, West Shaw, who teaches me something new every day and has been a constant support along this journey. And my fiancé, Bennett Molster who has weathered every decision, legal hurdle, late night, and moment of chaos that comes with building something from the ground up — but never once hesitated to encourage me to chase my dreams. Business is already booming, and I cannot wait to share more about what's ahead. If this journey has taught me anything, it's that leading with passion is never the wrong choice. When you pour your heart into what you do, it shows and good work, people, and opportunities will always find you. To solve "wicked problems," we need to move beyond siloed authority and toward System Leadership. In my opinion, shifting the focus from "my agency" to "the whole system" unlocks three critical benefits: 1. Radical Collaboration over Competition System leadership replaces the "turf war" mentality with shared goals. When leaders prioritize the collective outcome, we see streamlined services and a massive reduction in redundant spending. 2. Agility in Crisis Traditional hierarchies are often too slow for modern disruption. A systemic approach builds networks of trust before the crisis hits, allowing for rapid, coordinated responses that actually reach the citizens who need them most. 3. Sustainable, Long-Term Impact Short-term wins are easy; systemic change is hard. By understanding the root causes and interdependencies within a community, government leaders can implement policies that stick, rather than just "patching" symptoms.
